claim: Tissue homeostasis and regeneration in the Drosophila midgut is regulated by a diverse array of signaling pathways including the Hippo pathway.
source: Tissue homeostasis and regeneration in the Drosophila midgut is regulated by a diverse array of signaling pathways including the Hippo pathway.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about Drosophila midgut regulation.

claim: Hippo signaling restricts intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation by sequestering the transcription co-factor Yorkie (Yki) in the cytoplasm.
source: Hippo signaling restricts intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation by sequestering the transcription co-factor Yorkie (Yki) in the cytoplasm, a factor required for rapid ISC proliferation under injury-induced regeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about canonical Hippo signaling mechanisms.

claim: Yki is required for rapid ISC proliferation under injury-induced regeneration.
source: Hippo signaling restricts intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation by sequestering the transcription co-factor Yorkie (Yki) in the cytoplasm, a factor required for rapid ISC proliferation under injury-induced regeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about Yki function during regeneration.

claim: Lola is a transcription factor acting downstream of Hippo signaling to restrict ISC proliferation in a Yki-independent manner.
source: Here we identify Lola as a transcription factor acting downstream of Hippo signaling to restrict ISC proliferation in a Yki-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lola interacts with the Hippo signaling core kinase Warts (Wts).
source: Not only that Lola interacts with and is stabilized by the Hippo signaling core kinase Warts (Wts), Lola rescues the enhanced ISC proliferation upon Wts depletion via suppressing Dref and SkpA expressions.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Lola is stabilized by Warts (Wts).
source: Not only that Lola interacts with and is stabilized by the Hippo signaling core kinase Warts (Wts), Lola rescues the enhanced ISC proliferation upon Wts depletion via suppressing Dref and SkpA expressions.
evidence: This is supported by protein stability assays shown in Figure 6B-D and Figure 6K.

claim: Lola rescues the enhanced ISC proliferation upon Wts depletion via suppressing Dref and SkpA expressions.
source: Not only that Lola interacts with and is stabilized by the Hippo signaling core kinase Warts (Wts), Lola rescues the enhanced ISC proliferation upon Wts depletion via suppressing Dref and SkpA expressions.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lola is a non-canonical Hippo signaling component in regulating midgut homeostasis.
source: Our findings reveal that Lola is a non-canonical Hippo signaling component in regulating midgut homeostasis, providing insights on the mechanism of tissue maintenance and intestinal function.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by data showing Lola functions independently of Yki-Sd complex (Figure 4).

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut is functionally equivalent to the mammalian small intestine.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut, functionally equivalent to the mammalian small intestine, consists of a single epithelial layer where mature cell types differentiate apical-basally from the intestinal stem cells (ISCs) scattered along the basal side (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut consists of a single epithelial layer where mature cell types differentiate apical-basally from the intestinal stem cells (ISCs) scattered along the basal side.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut, functionally equivalent to the mammalian small intestine, consists of a single epithelial layer where mature cell types differentiate apical-basally from the intestinal stem cells (ISCs) scattered along the basal side (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2016.

claim: ISCs undergo asymmetric divisions that give rise to a renewable ISC and a non-dividing immature enteroblast (EB).
source: ISCs undergo asymmetric divisions that give rise to a renewable ISC and a non-dividing immature enteroblast (EB), which further differentiates into either an absorptive enterocyte (EC) or a secretory enteroendocrine (ee) cell (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006 and Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Enteroblasts differentiate into either an absorptive enterocyte (EC) or a secretory enteroendocrine (ee) cell.
source: ISCs undergo asymmetric divisions that give rise to a renewable ISC and a non-dividing immature enteroblast (EB), which further differentiates into either an absorptive enterocyte (EC) or a secretory enteroendocrine (ee) cell (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006 and Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Both ISCs and EBs express the Snail/Slug family transcription factor escargot.
source: Previous studies have shown that both ISCs and EBs, commonly referred as midgut precursors, express the Snail/Slug family transcription factor escargot (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006.

claim: ISCs are marked by the Notch (N) ligand Delta (Dl).
source: Whereas ISCs are marked by the Notch (N) ligand Delta (Dl) (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007), EBs can be labeled by a reporter of N signaling, Su(H)Gbe-lacZ (Su(H)-Z), due to the activation by neighboring ISCs (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007.

claim: EBs can be labeled by a reporter of N signaling, Su(H)Gbe-lacZ (Su(H)-Z), due to the activation by neighboring ISCs.
source: Whereas ISCs are marked by the Notch (N) ligand Delta (Dl) (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007), EBs can be labeled by a reporter of N signaling, Su(H)Gbe-lacZ (Su(H)-Z), due to the activation by neighboring ISCs (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006 and Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Terminally differentiated ECs are labeled by the class II POU domain transcription factor Pdm1 or Brush Border Myosin (MyoIA).
source: Terminally differentiated ECs, labeled by the class II POU domain transcription factor Pdm1 or Brush Border Myosin (MyoIA), acquire their large size and polyploid nuclei via endoreplication (Jiang et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2009 and Lee et al., 2009.

claim: ECs acquire their large size and polyploid nuclei via endoreplication.
source: Terminally differentiated ECs, labeled by the class II POU domain transcription factor Pdm1 or Brush Border Myosin (MyoIA), acquire their large size and polyploid nuclei via endoreplication (Jiang et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2009 and Lee et al., 2009.

claim: ee cells with small nuclei are specifically stained by Prospero (Pros).
source: On the other hand, ee cells with small nuclei are specifically stained by Prospero (Pros) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; and Singh et al., 2012.

claim: Midgut homeostasis is maintained via a basal level of ISC turnover to replace the cells loss during normal gut function.
source: Midgut homeostasis is maintained via a basal level of ISC turnover to replace the cells loss during normal gut function (Antonello et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Antonello et al., 2015 and Jiang et al., 2011.

claim: Upon stress or injury, ISCs undergo rapid proliferation in order to replenish enough cells in a limited time for regeneration.
source: Upon stress or injury, however, ISCs undergo rapid proliferation in order to replenish enough cells in a limited time for regeneration (Amcheslavsky et al., 2009; Buchon et al., 2010; Buchon et al., 2009b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Amcheslavsky et al., 2009; Buchon et al., 2010; and Buchon et al., 2009b.

claim: ISC proliferation processes are regulated by a number of signaling pathways such as N, Wingless, JAK-STAT and EGFR.
source: These processes are regulated by a number of signaling pathways such as N (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007), Wingless (Lin et al., 2008), JAK-STAT (Beebe et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2009) and EGFR (Buchon et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Hippo signaling plays pivotal roles in both Drosophila midgut homeostasis and regeneration via cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous mechanisms.
source: Particularly, Hippo signaling has been shown to play pivotal roles in both Drosophila midgut homeostasis and regeneration via cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous mechanisms (Karpowicz et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010; Staley and Irvine, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Karpowicz et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010; and Staley and Irvine, 2010.

claim: Hippo (Hpo) kinase phosphorylates and activates Warts (Wts) kinase via interaction with the scaffold protein Salvador (Sav).
source: The pathway consists of a core kinase cascade in which Hippo (Hpo) kinase phosphorylates and activates Warts (Wts) kinase via interaction with the scaffold protein Salvador (Sav).
evidence: This is established knowledge about canonical Hippo signaling.

claim: Wts interacts with Mob as tumor suppressor (Mats) to trigger phosphorylation of the transcription coactivator Yorkie (Yki).
source: Subsequently, Wts interacts with Mob as tumor suppressor (Mats) to trigger phosphorylation of the transcription coactivator Yorkie (Yki), blocking its translocation to form a complex with the transcription factor Scalloped (Sd) in the nucleus, thus inhibiting downstream signal transduction (Goulev et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2005; Justice et al., 1995; Oh and Irvine, 2008; Pantalacci et al., 2003; Udan et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Wts-mediated phosphorylation of Yki blocks its translocation to form a complex with the transcription factor Scalloped (Sd) in the nucleus.
source: Subsequently, Wts interacts with Mob as tumor suppressor (Mats) to trigger phosphorylation of the transcription coactivator Yorkie (Yki), blocking its translocation to form a complex with the transcription factor Scalloped (Sd) in the nucleus, thus inhibiting downstream signal transduction (Goulev et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2003; Huang et al., 2005; Justice et al., 1995; Oh and Irvine, 2008; Pantalacci et al., 2003; Udan et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003; Xu et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some upstream components regulate the Hippo signaling activity by controlling Wts protein levels.
source: Despite that Hippo signaling mainly transduces via triggering Wts phosphorylation (Udan et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003), previous studies indicate that some upstream components regulate the Hippo signaling activity by controlling Wts protein levels.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and inference from previous studies.

claim: The atypical cadherin Fat (Ft) functions as a Hippo component via regulating Wts protein stability.
source: The atypical cadherin Fat (Ft) (Cho et al., 2006), the atypical myosin Dachs (D) together with the LIM domain protein Zyxin (Zyx) (Rauskolb et al., 2011), and the tumor suppressor gene Scribble (Scrib) (Verghese et al., 2012) function as Hippo components via regulating Wts protein stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Cho et al., 2006.

claim: The atypical myosin Dachs (D) together with the LIM domain protein Zyxin (Zyx) function as Hippo components via regulating Wts protein stability.
source: The atypical cadherin Fat (Ft) (Cho et al., 2006), the atypical myosin Dachs (D) together with the LIM domain protein Zyxin (Zyx) (Rauskolb et al., 2011), and the tumor suppressor gene Scribble (Scrib) (Verghese et al., 2012) function as Hippo components via regulating Wts protein stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Rauskolb et al., 2011.

claim: The tumor suppressor gene Scribble (Scrib) functions as a Hippo component via regulating Wts protein stability.
source: The atypical cadherin Fat (Ft) (Cho et al., 2006), the atypical myosin Dachs (D) together with the LIM domain protein Zyxin (Zyx) (Rauskolb et al., 2011), and the tumor suppressor gene Scribble (Scrib) (Verghese et al., 2012) function as Hippo components via regulating Wts protein stability.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Verghese et al., 2012.

claim: During midgut homeostasis, Hippo signaling restricts ISC proliferation by sequestering Yki in the cytoplasm.
source: During midgut homeostasis, Hippo signaling restricts ISC proliferation by sequestering Yki in the cytoplasm, thereby deactivating downstream signaling.
evidence: This is established knowledge about canonical Hippo signaling function.

claim: Inactivation of Hpo or Wts leads to enhanced ISC proliferation.
source: Inactivation of Hpo or Wts leads to enhanced ISC proliferation, same as yki overexpression which activates EGFR and JAK-STAT pathways (in ECs, non-cell-autonomously) or promotes expression of target genes such as bantam microRNA (in ISCs, cell-autonomously) (Houtz et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2014; Nolo et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010; Staley and Irvine, 2010; Thompson and Cohen, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: yki overexpression activates EGFR and JAK-STAT pathways in ECs non-cell-autonomously.
source: Inactivation of Hpo or Wts leads to enhanced ISC proliferation, same as yki overexpression which activates EGFR and JAK-STAT pathways (in ECs, non-cell-autonomously) or promotes expression of target genes such as bantam microRNA (in ISCs, cell-autonomously) (Houtz et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2014; Nolo et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010; Staley and Irvine, 2010; Thompson and Cohen, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: yki overexpression promotes expression of target genes such as bantam microRNA in ISCs cell-autonomously.
source: Inactivation of Hpo or Wts leads to enhanced ISC proliferation, same as yki overexpression which activates EGFR and JAK-STAT pathways (in ECs, non-cell-autonomously) or promotes expression of target genes such as bantam microRNA (in ISCs, cell-autonomously) (Houtz et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2014; Nolo et al., 2006; Ren et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2010; Staley and Irvine, 2010; Thompson and Cohen, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Yki-Sd complex is considered as the major mediator for injury-induced midgut regeneration.
source: In addition, the Yki-Sd complex is considered as the major mediator for injury-induced midgut regeneration, as loss of Yki in either ISCs or ECs blocks DSS- or infection-stimulated ISC proliferation, respectively (Cai et al., 2010; Karpowicz et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Cai et al., 2010; Karpowicz et al., 2010; and Ren et al., 2010.

claim: Loss of Yki in either ISCs or ECs blocks DSS- or infection-stimulated ISC proliferation.
source: In addition, the Yki-Sd complex is considered as the major mediator for injury-induced midgut regeneration, as loss of Yki in either ISCs or ECs blocks DSS- or infection-stimulated ISC proliferation, respectively (Cai et al., 2010; Karpowicz et al., 2010; Ren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Cai et al., 2010; Karpowicz et al., 2010; and Ren et al., 2010.

claim: Neither Yki nor Sd depletion causes defects in ISC basal proliferation.
source: Despite abundant evidence underlying the significance of Hippo signaling during midgut homeostasis and regeneration, neither Yki nor Sd depletion causes defects in ISC basal proliferation, raising the controversies whether the Yki-Sd complex truly executes downstream Hippo signaling during midgut homeostasis as it does in regeneration.
evidence: This is an observation that raises questions about canonical Hippo signaling during homeostasis, supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 4.

claim: longitudinals lacking (lola) is a transcription factor implicated in axon growth and guidance.
source: longitudinals lacking (lola) is a transcription factor implicated in axon growth and guidance (Crowner et al., 2002; Giniger et al., 1994), ovary cell apoptosis (Bass et al., 2007), germline/neuron stem cell differentiation and maintenance (Davies et al., 2013; Silva et al., 2016; Southall et al., 2014) and wing margin development (Bass et al., 2007; Krupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Crowner et al., 2002 and Giniger et al., 1994.

claim: lola is implicated in ovary cell apoptosis.
source: longitudinals lacking (lola) is a transcription factor implicated in axon growth and guidance (Crowner et al., 2002; Giniger et al., 1994), ovary cell apoptosis (Bass et al., 2007), germline/neuron stem cell differentiation and maintenance (Davies et al., 2013; Silva et al., 2016; Southall et al., 2014) and wing margin development (Bass et al., 2007; Krupp et al., 2005).

claim: lola cooperates with Dl to induce the formation of metastatic tumors.
source: It also cooperates with Dl to induce the formation of metastatic tumors and regulates cell fate in Drosophila eye by antagonizing N signaling (Ferres-Marco et al., 2006; Zheng and Carthew, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ferres-Marco et al., 2006 and Zheng and Carthew, 2008.

claim: lola regulates cell fate in Drosophila eye by antagonizing N signaling.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ferres-Marco et al., 2006 and Zheng and Carthew, 2008.

claim: The protein product of lola contains a N-terminal BTB or POZ domain and one or two C-terminal zinc finger motifs.
source: Despite the presence of more than 20 alternatively-spliced isoforms, the protein product of lola contains a N-terminal BTB or POZ domain and one or two C-terminal zinc finger motifs, indicating that Lola is a Cullin-3 (Cul3)-based substrate adaptor that also binds DNA (Furukawa et al., 2003; Geyer et al., 2003; Goeke et al., 2003; Horiuchi et al., 2003; Ohsako et al., 2003; Pintard et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Lola is a Cullin-3 (Cul3)-based substrate adaptor that also binds DNA.
source: Despite the presence of more than 20 alternatively-spliced isoforms, the protein product of lola contains a N-terminal BTB or POZ domain and one or two C-terminal zinc finger motifs, indicating that Lola is a Cullin-3 (Cul3)-based substrate adaptor that also binds DNA (Furukawa et al., 2003; Geyer et al., 2003; Goeke et al., 2003; Horiuchi et al., 2003; Ohsako et al., 2003; Pintard et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features of Lola, supported by citations.

claim: Expression of wts RNAi resulted in an increase in the number of GFP+ cells in the posterior part of the midgut.
source: Expression of wts RNAi (esgts > wts RNAi) resulted in an increase in the number of GFP+ cells in the posterior part of the midgut, indicating that reduced wts expression leads to an expansion of the precursor cell population (Figure 1B–B' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1B-B'.

claim: Reduced wts expression leads to an expansion of the precursor cell population.
source: Expression of wts RNAi (esgts > wts RNAi) resulted in an increase in the number of GFP+ cells in the posterior part of the midgut, indicating that reduced wts expression leads to an expansion of the precursor cell population (Figure 1B–B' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference from the observation of increased GFP+ cells shown in Figure 1B-B'.

claim: Reduced yki expression does not lead to obvious difference in the number of GFP+ cells.
source: Consistent with previous results, reduced yki expression (esgts > yki RNAi) does not lead to obvious difference in the number of GFP+ cells, suggesting that Yki is not required for overall midgut homeostasis (Figure 1C–C').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1C-C'.

claim: Yki is not required for overall midgut homeostasis.
source: Consistent with previous results, reduced yki expression (esgts > yki RNAi) does not lead to obvious difference in the number of GFP+ cells, suggesting that Yki is not required for overall midgut homeostasis (Figure 1C–C').
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that yki RNAi does not affect GFP+ cell numbers shown in Figure 1C-C'.

claim: Downregulating wts expression in ISCs and EBs leads to an obvious increase in p-H3+ cell number.
source: Immunostaining with antibodies against phospho-Histone 3 (p-H3) that marks mitotic cells derived from ISCs indicated an obvious increase in p-H3+ cell number when downregulating wts expression in ISCs and EBs (esgts > wts RNAi, Figure 1E), suggesting that the expansion in the precursor cell population in Figure 1B is due to enhanced ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The expansion in the precursor cell population upon wts RNAi is due to enhanced ISC proliferation.
source: Immunostaining with antibodies against phospho-Histone 3 (p-H3) that marks mitotic cells derived from ISCs indicated an obvious increase in p-H3+ cell number when downregulating wts expression in ISCs and EBs (esgts > wts RNAi, Figure 1E), suggesting that the expansion in the precursor cell population in Figure 1B is due to enhanced ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference from the increased p-H3+ cell numbers shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Co-expression of yki and wts RNAi does not suppress the growth of precursor cell population induced by wts RNAi.
source: Unexpectedly, co-expression of yki and wts RNAi suppressed neither the growth of precursor cell population nor the enhanced proliferation induced by wts RNAi, suggesting that Wts mediates ISC proliferation independently of Yki (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Co-expression of yki and wts RNAi does not suppress the enhanced proliferation induced by wts RNAi.
source: Unexpectedly, co-expression of yki and wts RNAi suppressed neither the growth of precursor cell population nor the enhanced proliferation induced by wts RNAi, suggesting that Wts mediates ISC proliferation independently of Yki (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Wts mediates ISC proliferation independently of Yki.
source: Unexpectedly, co-expression of yki and wts RNAi suppressed neither the growth of precursor cell population nor the enhanced proliferation induced by wts RNAi, suggesting that Wts mediates ISC proliferation independently of Yki (Figure 1D–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The number of Dl-labeled ISCs was increased in wtsx1 clones.
source: Interestingly, the number of Dl-labeled ISCs was increased in wtsx1 clones, indicating that ISCs are over proliferative (Figure 1F–G' and I).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 1F-G' and I.

claim: ISCs are over proliferative in wtsx1 clones.
source: Interestingly, the number of Dl-labeled ISCs was increased in wtsx1 clones, indicating that ISCs are over proliferative (Figure 1F–G' and I).
evidence: This is an inference from the increased Dl+ cell numbers shown in Figure 1F-G' and I.

claim: Simultaneous expression of yki RNAi in wtsx1 clones did not restore the elevated Dl+ cell number.
source: Consistent to our wts RNAi results, simultaneous expression of yki RNAi in these clones did not restore the elevated Dl+ cell number (Figure 1H–I), suggesting that the reduced yki expression does not block wtsx1-induced ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Reduced yki expression does not block wtsx1-induced ISC proliferation.
source: Consistent to our wts RNAi results, simultaneous expression of yki RNAi in these clones did not restore the elevated Dl+ cell number (Figure 1H–I), suggesting that the reduced yki expression does not block wtsx1-induced ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 1H-I.

claim: Expression of wts RNAi by MS1096-Gal4 resulted in larger wing size.
source: Using Drosophila wing as a model, expression of wts RNAi by MS1096-Gal4 resulted in larger wing size, a phenotype rescued by yki RNAi co-expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-K.

claim: The larger wing size phenotype induced by wts RNAi is rescued by yki RNAi co-expression.
source: Using Drosophila wing as a model, expression of wts RNAi by MS1096-Gal4 resulted in larger wing size, a phenotype rescued by yki RNAi co-expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-K.

claim: Yki functions together with Wts in controlling the wing size.
source: These results suggest that Yki functions together with Wts in controlling the wing size, a mechanism that differs from gut homeostasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K).
evidence: This is an inference from the wing size rescue experiment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G-K.

claim: The mechanism of Wts and Yki in controlling wing size differs from gut homeostasis.
source: These results suggest that Yki functions together with Wts in controlling the wing size, a mechanism that differs from gut homeostasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–K).
evidence: This is an inference comparing wing and gut phenotypes.

claim: Clones expressing wts RNAi were bigger than the control.
source: Under this condition, we found that clones expressing wts RNAi were bigger than the control, and the size was not or only slightly affected by the presence of ykiB5 or sd ∆B1, respectively (Figure 1J–N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–P).
evidence: This is supported by clone size quantification data shown in Figure 1J-N.

claim: The size of clones expressing wts RNAi was not or only slightly affected by the presence of ykiB5 or sd ∆B1.
source: Under this condition, we found that clones expressing wts RNAi were bigger than the control, and the size was not or only slightly affected by the presence of ykiB5 or sd ∆B1, respectively (Figure 1J–N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L–P).
evidence: This is supported by clone size quantification data shown in Figure 1J-N and Figure 1—figure supplement 1L-P.

claim: Wts-mediated Hippo signaling regulates midgut homeostasis independently of the Yki-Sd transcriptional complex.
source: Taken together, these results indicate a non-canonical mechanism regulating midgut homeostasis by Hippo signaling. The regulatory mechanism depends on Wts function, yet is independent of the Yki-Sd transcriptional complex in Drosophila midgut.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from multiple genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of lola RNAi resulted in an increased number of GFP+ cells in the posterior midgut.
source: Interestingly, expression of two independent RNAi lines VDRC12574 (Figure 2) and NIG12052 R-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), both target and abolish lola expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), resulted in an increased number of GFP+ and p-H3+ cells in the posterior midgut (Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).

claim: Expression of lola RNAi resulted in an increased number of p-H3+ cells in the posterior midgut.

evidence: This is supported by microscopy and quantification data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The p-H3+ cells were dually labeled with Dl, suggesting that these cells are proliferative ISCs.
source: Moreover, the p-H3+ cells were dually labeled with Dl, suggesting that these cells are proliferative ISCs (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is an inference from the co-localization data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Reducing lola expression in gut precursor cells promotes ISC proliferation.
source: These results indicate that reducing lola expression in gut precursor cells promotes ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference from the increased p-H3+ and GFP+ cell numbers shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: MARCM lola5D2 mutant clones were bigger in size compared to the control.

claim: lola5D2 mutant clones have a growth advantage due to ISC hyperproliferation when lola expression is reduced.
source: In addition, MARCM lola5D2 (a hypomorphic allele) mutant clones were bigger in size compared to the control (Figure 2D–E'''), indicating a growth advantage due to ISC hyperproliferation when lola expression is reduced.

claim: lola5D2 mutant clones contained Pdm1+ ECs and Pros+ ee cells.
source: As shown in Figure 2E–E''', these lola5D2 mutant clones contained Pdm1+ ECs and Pros+ ee cells, suggesting that Lola activity is not required for ISC differentiation.

claim: Lola activity is not required for ISC differentiation.
source: As shown in Figure 2E–E''', these lola5D2 mutant clones contained Pdm1+ ECs and Pros+ ee cells, suggesting that Lola activity is not required for ISC differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference from the presence of differentiated cell types in lola5D2 clones shown in Figure 2E-E'''.

claim: Expressing lola RNAi in ECs dramatically promoted ISC proliferation.
source: Compared with the control groups, expressing either lola RNAi in ECs dramatically promoted ISC proliferation, as indicated by the increased Dl+ and p-H3+ cell number (Figure 2F–H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: Reducing lola expression in ECs resulted in gut hypertrophy associated with multi-layer of intestinal cells.
source: Moreover, reducing lola expression in ECs resulted in gut hypertrophy associated with multi-layer of intestinal cells (Figure 2I–J''), possibly a consequence of hyperproliferation.
evidence: This is supported by cross-section microscopy data shown in Figure 2I-J''.

claim: Gut hypertrophy upon lola RNAi in ECs is possibly a consequence of hyperproliferation.
source: Moreover, reducing lola expression in ECs resulted in gut hypertrophy associated with multi-layer of intestinal cells (Figure 2I–J''), possibly a consequence of hyperproliferation.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed phenotype shown in Figure 2I-J''.

claim: Lola has a non-cell-autonomous role in regulating ISC proliferation during midgut homeostasis.
source: Based on the findings that ECs interact with ISCs and regulate their proliferation (Gervais and Bardin, 2017), these results suggest a non-cell-autonomous role of Lola in regulating ISC proliferation during midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the EC-specific lola RNAi experiments shown in Figure 2F-H, supported by citation to Gervais and Bardin, 2017.

claim: Reducing lola expression in ECs did not induce non-specific apoptosis in the posterior midgut.
source: Importantly, reducing lola expression in ECs did not induce non-specific apoptosis in the posterior midgut (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I''), indicating that lola RNAi promotes ISC proliferation via a specific signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I''.

claim: lola RNAi promotes ISC proliferation via a specific signaling pathway.
source: Importantly, reducing lola expression in ECs did not induce non-specific apoptosis in the posterior midgut (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H–I''), indicating that lola RNAi promotes ISC proliferation via a specific signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of apoptosis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H-I''.

claim: Lola is required in both precursor cells and ECs for ISC proliferation and midgut homeostasis.
source: Altogether, Lola is required in both precursor cells and ECs for ISC proliferation and midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs caused a significant increase in the levels of dpERK.
source: Interestingly, Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs caused a significant increase in the levels of dpERK, the dephosphorylated active form of MAPK (Gabay et al., 1997), and the mRNA levels of EGFR ligands Spitz (Spi), Vein (Vn), and Krn, all indicating EGFR activation (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs caused a significant increase in the mRNA levels of EGFR ligands Spitz (Spi), Vein (Vn), and Krn.
source: Interestingly, Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs caused a significant increase in the levels of dpERK, the dephosphorylated active form of MAPK (Gabay et al., 1997), and the mRNA levels of EGFR ligands Spitz (Spi), Vein (Vn), and Krn, all indicating EGFR activation (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Lola depletion activates EGFR signaling.
source: Interestingly, Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs caused a significant increase in the levels of dpERK, the dephosphorylated active form of MAPK (Gabay et al., 1997), and the mRNA levels of EGFR ligands Spitz (Spi), Vein (Vn), and Krn, all indicating EGFR activation (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is an inference from the increased dpERK levels and EGFR ligand expression shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs activates JAK-STAT signaling.
source: Moreover, Lola depletion in either precursors or ECs activates JAK-STAT signaling as indicated by the elevated expressions of JAK-STAT ligand Upd3 and Stat-GFP, a multimerized Stat92E reporter driving the expression of a destabilized GFP to monitor JAK-STAT activity (Bach et al., 2007) (Figure 3F–M).
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3F-M.

claim: mRNA levels of Upds (Upd, Upd2, and Upd3), and the JAK-STAT target Socs36E were elevated dramatically upon Lola depletion.
source: Consistently, mRNA levels of Upds (Upd, Upd2, and Upd3), and the JAK-STAT target Socs36E were elevated dramatically upon Lola depletion (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Expression levels of the microRNA bantam were elevated upon Lola depletion.
source: Furthermore, expression levels of the microRNA bantam, a canonical downstream target of Hippo signaling essential for cell-autonomous ISC proliferation (Huang et al., 2014), were also elevated upon Lola depletion (Figure 3O–P''').
evidence: This is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 3O-P'''.

claim: Loss of Lola activates EGFR, JAK-STAT, and microRNA bantam signaling.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of Lola activates EGFR, JAK-STAT, and microRNA bantam signaling, suggesting that Lola regulates ISC proliferation likely via mechanisms involving Hippo signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the signaling pathway activation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Lola regulates ISC proliferation likely via mechanisms involving Hippo signaling.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of Lola activates EGFR, JAK-STAT, and microRNA bantam signaling, suggesting that Lola regulates ISC proliferation likely via mechanisms involving Hippo signaling.
evidence: This is speculation based on the similarity of downstream pathway activation to Hippo signaling inactivation.

claim: Lola depletion does not affect yki mRNA levels.
source: Real-time PCR analysis of total RNAs from Actints > lola RNAi guts revealed no significant difference in yki mRNA levels between control and RNAi samples, suggesting that Lola does not affect yki transcription (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lola does not affect yki transcription.
source: Real-time PCR analysis of total RNAs from Actints > lola RNAi guts revealed no significant difference in yki mRNA levels between control and RNAi samples, suggesting that Lola does not affect yki transcription (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference from the RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No Yki protein accumulation was detected in lola5D2 mutant gut clones.
source: No Yki protein accumulation was detected in lola5D2 mutant gut clones, suggesting that Lola does not affect Yki protein levels either (Figure 4B–C').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B-C'.

claim: Lola does not affect Yki protein levels.
source: No Yki protein accumulation was detected in lola5D2 mutant gut clones, suggesting that Lola does not affect Yki protein levels either (Figure 4B–C').
evidence: This is an inference from the immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B-C'.

claim: Co-expression of either yki or sd RNAi with lola RNAi in ISCs did not suppress the increase in p-H3+ cell number induced by lola RNAi alone.
source: Genetic interaction analysis indicated that co-expression of either yki or sd RNAi with lola RNAi in ISCs did not suppress the increase in p-H3+ cell number induced by lola RNAi alone (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–F').
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: MARCM clones of double mutant lola5D2 and ykiB5 exhibited no significant difference in clone size compared to lola5D2.
source: Furthermore, MARCM clones of double mutant lola5D2 and ykiB5 exhibited no significant difference in clone size compared to lola5D2 (Figure 4E–H').
evidence: This is supported by clone size data shown in Figure 4E-H'.

claim: MARCM sd∆B1 mutant clones expressing lola RNAi were larger in size.
source: MARCM sd∆B1 mutant clones expressing lola RNAi were similarly larger in size, suggesting that Sd depletion does not suppress lola RNAi-induced ISC proliferation (Figure 4I–L').
evidence: This is supported by clone size data shown in Figure 4I-L'.

claim: Sd depletion does not suppress lola RNAi-induced ISC proliferation.
source: MARCM sd∆B1 mutant clones expressing lola RNAi were similarly larger in size, suggesting that Sd depletion does not suppress lola RNAi-induced ISC proliferation (Figure 4I–L').
evidence: This is an inference from the clone size data shown in Figure 4I-L'.

claim: Lola restricts ISC proliferation independently of the Yki-Sd transcriptional complex.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Lola restricts ISC proliferation independently of the Yki-Sd transcriptional complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Lola mainly binds to the regions around transcription start sites (TSS) and promoters.
source: Analysis of the Lola binding profiles revealed that Lola mainly binds to the regions around transcription start sites (TSS) and promoters.
evidence: This is an inference from ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: ChIP assay and real-time PCR showed dramatic enrichment of Lola in promoter regions of Oli, ec, Dref, and 3'UTR regions of pdm3 and SkpA.
source: Results from ChIP assay and real-time PCR showed dramatic enrichment of Lola in promoter regions of Oli, ec, Dref, and 3'UTR regions of pdm3 and SkpA.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lola knockdown by dsRNA significantly reduced the enrichment of Lola on target gene regions.
source: As a negative control, Lola knockdown by dsRNA significantly reduced the enrichment (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: mRNA levels of pdm3, ec, Dref, and SkpA were upregulated when reducing lola expression.
source: To validate these results in vivo, total RNAs from Actints > lola RNAi guts were collected and analyzed. Similarly, mRNA levels of pdm3, ec, Dref, and SkpA were upregulated when reducing lola expression, suggesting that Lola suppresses the expression of these genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lola suppresses the expression of pdm3, ec, Dref, and SkpA.
source: To validate these results in vivo, total RNAs from Actints > lola RNAi guts were collected and analyzed. Similarly, mRNA levels of pdm3, ec, Dref, and SkpA were upregulated when reducing lola expression, suggesting that Lola suppresses the expression of these genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference from the RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Activities of Dref and SkpA reporters were dramatically inhibited by Lola but not Lola∆ZF12.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, activities of these reporters were dramatically inhibited by Lola but not Lola∆ZF12, a truncated form of Lola that does not bind to DNA.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dref protein levels were significantly elevated in lola5D2 mutant clones.
source: In addition, Dref protein levels were significantly elevated in lola5D2 mutant clones (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and quantification data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Lola regulates the expression of Dref and SkpA, and represses their transcription.
source: In summary, these results suggest that Lola regulates the expression of Dref and SkpA, and represses their transcription.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the ChIP, RT-PCR, and reporter assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Knock down of either Dref or SkpA significantly rescued the increase in GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by lola RNAi.
source: As expected, knock down of either Dref or SkpA significantly rescued the increase in GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by lola RNAi (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H'), indicating that Lola restricts ISC proliferation via regulating Dref or SkpA expression levels.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Lola restricts ISC proliferation via regulating Dref or SkpA expression levels.
source: As expected, knock down of either Dref or SkpA significantly rescued the increase in GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by lola RNAi (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–H'), indicating that Lola restricts ISC proliferation via regulating Dref or SkpA expression levels.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic rescue data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Fg-Lola protein levels were significantly increased only in the presence of Myc-Wts.
source: Interestingly, Fg-Lola protein levels were significantly increased only in the presence of Myc-Wts (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Fg-Lola was increasingly stabilized when adding increasing amount of Myc-Wts.
source: In addition, Fg-Lola was increasingly stabilized when adding increasing amount of Myc-Wts, indicating that Wts regulates Lola protein levels in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Wts regulates Lola protein levels in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: In addition, Fg-Lola was increasingly stabilized when adding increasing amount of Myc-Wts, indicating that Wts regulates Lola protein levels in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference from the dose-response data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fg-Lola proteins exhibited a rapid turnover rate with a half-life of approximately 2 hr.
source: As shown in Figure 6C–D, Fg-Lola proteins exhibited a rapid turnover rate with a half-life of approximately 2 hr, while Myc-Wts prolonged Fg-Lola protein half-life to about 6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by CHX chase assay data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Myc-Wts prolonged Fg-Lola protein half-life to about 6 hr.
source: As shown in Figure 6C–D, Fg-Lola proteins exhibited a rapid turnover rate with a half-life of approximately 2 hr, while Myc-Wts prolonged Fg-Lola protein half-life to about 6 hr.
evidence: This is supported by CHX chase assay data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: UPS inhibitors, but not lysosome inhibitors, protected Fg-Lola from degradation.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, UPS inhibitors, but not lysosome inhibitors, protected Fg-Lola from degradation, indicating that UPS plays a major role in regulating Lola protein stability.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: UPS plays a major role in regulating Lola protein stability.
source: As shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, UPS inhibitors, but not lysosome inhibitors, protected Fg-Lola from degradation, indicating that UPS plays a major role in regulating Lola protein stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Lola ubiquitination levels were reduced in the presence of Wts.
source: In addition, Lola ubiquitination levels were reduced in the presence of Wts as shown by results from the in vivo ubiquitination assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Wts regulates Lola protein stability by protecting Lola from UPS-mediated degradation.
source: These results demonstrate that Wts regulates Lola protein stability by protecting Lola from UPS-mediated degradation, hence the possibility of Hippo signaling regulating Lola function.
evidence: This is an inference from the stability and ubiquitination data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lola and Wts reciprocally interacted.
source: As shown in Figure 6E, Lola and Wts reciprocally interacted, validating a physical interaction between two proteins.
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wts interacts with endogenous Lola.
source: Co-IP analysis of S2 cells expressing Myc-Wts using the anti-Lola antibody for IP pulled down Myc-Wts, further demonstrating that Wts interacts with endogenous Lola (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Fg-LolaC, but not Fg-LolaN, co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-Wts.
source: Co-IP results indicated that Fg-LolaC, but not Fg-LolaN, co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-Wts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that Wts interacts with Lola C-terminus.
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Wts interacts with Lola C-terminus.
source: Co-IP results indicated that Fg-LolaC, but not Fg-LolaN, co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-Wts (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that Wts interacts with Lola C-terminus.
evidence: This is an inference from the Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Deletion of either ZF1 or ZF2 or both in Lola C-terminus did not affect binding between Wts and Lola.
source: Deletion of either ZF1 or ZF2 or both in Lola C-terminus did not affect binding between Wts and Lola, suggesting that Wts-Lola interaction does not require DNA binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Wts-Lola interaction does not require DNA binding.
source: Deletion of either ZF1 or ZF2 or both in Lola C-terminus did not affect binding between Wts and Lola, suggesting that Wts-Lola interaction does not require DNA binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and C).
evidence: This is an inference from the Co-IP data with zinc finger deletion mutants shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Wts does not affect Lola-DNA binding.
source: Furthermore, ChIP-qPCR analysis revealed no detectable change of Lola enrichment on Dref or SkpA binding regions when co-expressing Wts in S2 cells (Figure 6G), indicating that Wts does not affect Lola-DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Wts interacts with Lola C-terminus independently of Lola binding to DNA.
source: In toto, these results suggest that Wts interacts with Lola C-terminus independently of Lola binding to DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the Co-IP and ChIP data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lola exhibited no shift in molecular weight when analyzed by the phos-tag gels.
source: Surprisingly, Lola exhibited no shift in molecular weight when analyzed by the phos-tag gels (Figure 6E), suggesting that Wts interacts with Lola in a manner independent of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wts interacts with Lola in a manner independent of phosphorylation.
source: Surprisingly, Lola exhibited no shift in molecular weight when analyzed by the phos-tag gels (Figure 6E), suggesting that Wts interacts with Lola in a manner independent of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is an inference from the phos-tag gel data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Wts KD interacted with Lola.
source: Not only that Wts KD interacted with Lola by Co-IP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), Wts KD stabilized Lola similarly as the wild-type Wts (data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Wts kinase activity is not essential for binding to Lola.
source: These results suggest that Wts kinase activity is not essential for binding to Lola and does not affect Lola protein stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the Wts KD interaction and stability data.

claim: Wts kinase activity does not affect Lola protein stability.
source: These results suggest that Wts kinase activity is not essential for binding to Lola and does not affect Lola protein stability.
evidence: This is an inference from the Wts KD stability data.

claim: Both total amount and the S168 phosphorylation level of Yki co-immunoprecipitated with Wts remained unaffected in the presence or absence of Fg-Lola.
source: In our hands, both total amount and the S168 phosphorylation level of Yki co-immunoprecipitated with Wts remained unaffected in the presence or absence of Fg-Lola, suggesting that Wts-Lola interaction does not affect Wts-Yki interaction and Wts-mediated Yki phosphorylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Wts-Lola interaction does not affect Wts-Yki interaction and Wts-mediated Yki phosphorylation.
source: In our hands, both total amount and the S168 phosphorylation level of Yki co-immunoprecipitated with Wts remained unaffected in the presence or absence of Fg-Lola, suggesting that Wts-Lola interaction does not affect Wts-Yki interaction and Wts-mediated Yki phosphorylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is an inference from the Co-IP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Wts binds to Lola directly to moderate its turnover rate, a process independent of Wts kinase activity, Lola DNA binding, Wts-Yki interaction, and Wts-mediated Yki phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Wts binds to Lola directly to moderate its turnover rate, a process independent of Wts kinase activity, Lola DNA binding, Wts-Yki interaction, and Wts-mediated Yki phosphorylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from multiple biochemical experiments shown in Figure 6 and supplementary figures.

claim: Expression of Wts fused with a C-terminal nuclear localization signal (NLS) (WtsNLS) caused a remarkable increase in Lola protein levels.
source: Our results showed that expression of Wts fused with a C-terminal nuclear localization signal (NLS) (WtsNLS) caused a remarkable increase in Lola protein levels, suggesting that WtsNLS stabilizes Lola in the nucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D), whereas the expression of Wts fused with a C-terminal nuclear export signal (NES) (WtsNES) only reduced the increased Lola protein levels partially (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D), suggesting the possibility of Lola translocating to cytoplasm where it is protected by Wts.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: WtsNLS stabilizes Lola in the nucleus.
source: Our results showed that expression of Wts fused with a C-terminal nuclear localization signal (NLS) (WtsNLS) caused a remarkable increase in Lola protein levels, suggesting that WtsNLS stabilizes Lola in the nucleus (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D), whereas the expression of Wts fused with a C-terminal nuclear export signal (NES) (WtsNES) only reduced the increased Lola protein levels partially (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–D), suggesting the possibility of Lola translocating to cytoplasm where it is protected by Wts.
evidence: This is an inference from the WtsNLS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Wts interacts with Lola both in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: These results indicate that Wts interacts with Lola both in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
evidence: This is an inference from the WtsNLS and WtsNES data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Lola is ubiquitously expressed in all cell types in the midgut.
source: Immunostainings showed that Lola is ubiquitously expressed in all cell types in the midgut and absent in the lola5D2 MARCM clones (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–B''').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-B'''.

claim: A dramatic decrease in the anti-Lola staining was detected in both flip-out clones expressing wts RNAi and wtsx1 MARCM clones in midguts.
source: Consistent with the cell culture data, a dramatic decrease in the anti-Lola staining was also detected in both flip-out clones expressing wts RNAi using the driver hsflp; act >CD2>Gal4; UAS-Dicer2, UAS-GFP (AG4; Dcr2GFP > wts RNAi) and wtsx1 MARCM clones in midguts (Figure 6H–J and Figure 6—figure supplement 3C–D''').
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6H-J and Figure 6—figure supplement 3C-D'''.

claim: wts overexpression increased Lola protein levels.
source: Furthermore, endogenous Lola protein levels were analyzed by Western blot using gut extracts that ubiquitously express lola, lola RNAi, wts, or wts RNAi. Similar to lola overexpression, wts overexpression increased Lola protein levels (Figure 6K).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: Wts regulates Lola protein levels in vivo.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Wts regulates Lola protein levels in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the in vivo immunostaining and Western blot data shown in Figure 6.

claim: lola overexpression dramatically reduced the increase in GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by wts RNAi.
source: Whereas reduced yki expression did not rescue the increase in the GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by esgts > wts RNAi (Figure 1A–E), lola overexpression dramatically reduced this increase (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D').
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: lola overexpression blocks the hyperproliferation induced by wts RNAi both cell-autonomously and non-cell-autonomously.
source: Similar reduction was detected in midguts expressing lola and wts RNAi in ECs (MyoIAts > lola; wts RNAi, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E). These results indicate that lola overexpression blocks the hyperproliferation induced by wts RNAi both cell-autonomously and non-cell-autonomously.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Expressing lola in GFP+wtsx1 MARCM clones dramatically reduced the clone size.
source: To further validate our observation, expressing lola in GFP+wtsx1 MARCM clones that exhibited the overgrowth phenotype dramatically reduced the clone size (Figure 7B–F).
evidence: This is supported by clone size quantification data shown in Figure 7B-F.

claim: wts overexpression in lola5D2 MARCM clones did not affect the increased clone size.
source: On the other hand, wts overexpression in lola5D2 MARCM clones did not affect the increased clone size (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by clone size data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Lola is essential for Wts function in midgut homeostasis.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Lola is essential for Wts function in midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: Dref and SkpA mRNA levels were elevated in wtsx1 clonal midguts.
source: Furthermore, Dref and SkpA mRNA levels were also elevated in wtsx1 clonal midguts (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Co-expression of SkpA or Dref RNAi in wts RNAi midguts dramatically reduced the increase in the GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number.
source: Genetic interaction analysis between wts and Dref or SkpA showed that co-expression of SkpA or Dref RNAi in wts RNAi midguts dramatically reduced the increase in the GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and G–H'), indicating that SkpA and Dref are both required for Wts function in midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SkpA and Dref are both required for Wts function in midgut homeostasis.
source: Genetic interaction analysis between wts and Dref or SkpA showed that co-expression of SkpA or Dref RNAi in wts RNAi midguts dramatically reduced the increase in the GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E and G–H'), indicating that SkpA and Dref are both required for Wts function in midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic rescue data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Wts stabilizes Lola such that SkpA and Dref expressions are transcriptionally suppressed, thereby restricting ISC proliferation.
source: These results support our hypothesis that Wts stabilizes Lola such that SkpA and Dref expressions are transcriptionally suppressed, thereby restricting ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the genetic and biochemical data shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: A high degree of similarity was detected between samples from wts and lola RNAi based on DEG heatmap and hierarchical cluster analysis.
source: Based on the DEG heatmap and hierarchical cluster analysis, a high degree of similarity was detected between samples from wts and lola RNAi, suggesting strong functional correlation between Wts and Lola, but not Yki and Lola, in regulating midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: There is strong functional correlation between Wts and Lola in regulating midgut homeostasis.
source: Based on the DEG heatmap and hierarchical cluster analysis, a high degree of similarity was detected between samples from wts and lola RNAi, suggesting strong functional correlation between Wts and Lola, but not Yki and Lola, in regulating midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq clustering analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: lola overexpression did not rescue the elevated GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by yki overexpression.
source: On the other hand, lola overexpression did not rescue the elevated GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by yki overexpression (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–E), reinforcing the notion that Lola restricts ISC proliferation in an Yki-independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Lola restricts ISC proliferation in an Yki-independent manner.
source: On the other hand, lola overexpression did not rescue the elevated GFP+ and p-H3+ cell number induced by yki overexpression (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–E), reinforcing the notion that Lola restricts ISC proliferation in an Yki-independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A-E.

claim: Wts regulates Lola and Yki in different means.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that while Wts regulates Lola and Yki in different means, Lola are functionally similar with Wts.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the differential regulation mechanisms shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lola is functionally similar with Wts.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that while Wts regulates Lola and Yki in different means, Lola are functionally similar with Wts.
evidence: This is an inference from the RNA-seq similarity and genetic interaction data.

claim: Yki and Lola regulate the expression of different target genes, and direct different transcription programs in the process of Hippo-mediated ISC proliferation and midgut homeostasis.
source: Yki and Lola regulate the expression of different target genes, and direct different transcription programs in the process of Hippo-mediated ISC proliferation and midgut homeostasis (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the RNA-seq and genetic data shown throughout the manuscript.
